idea-validator.name: Business idea validator
idea-validator.blurb: Score your idea out of 100 and see what to test first.

idea-validator.q1: How do I know if my business idea is good?
idea-validator.a1: Check proof of demand first: are people already paying for something similar, or have they paid or signed up for yours? Then check whether a sale is worth enough, how crowded the market is, what it costs to start and how you will reach customers. The validator scores all of these.
idea-validator.a2: Eight answers make a readiness score: proof of demand counts most (20%), then your edge and how you reach customers (15% each), then price, competition, startup cost, time to first sale and the market trend (10% each). If your idea matches one in our ideas list, its search-data outlook score counts for a quarter of the total.
idea-validator.q3: Where does the market benchmark come from?
idea-validator.a3: From the cv.cm ideas channel: four years of Google Ads Keyword Planner searches in eight languages for 40 business ideas, refreshed monthly. Type your idea and the closest one is picked, or choose it from the list.
idea-validator.a4: No. The scoring and the matching run in this tab. Nothing you type is uploaded or stored.
idea-validator.q5: Does a high score mean my business will succeed?
idea-validator.a5: No. It means the basics look sound. The only real test is customers paying, so use the steps it suggests to test cheaply before you spend real money.

idea-validator.lead: Score a business idea in three steps.
idea-validator.s1b: Type it in a few words. If it matches one of our 40 ideas, its search-data score is used as the market benchmark; you can also pick one from the list.
idea-validator.s2b: Choose the closest option for proof of demand, price, competition, startup cost, time to first sale, your edge, how you reach customers and the market trend.
idea-validator.s3b: See the score out of 100, your strengths and weak spots, and three cheap tests for the weakest one. Copy the result to keep it.

verdict.strong: The basics look sound. Test it with real customers now, before you polish anything.
verdict.promising: Worth pursuing if you fix the weak spots below first.
verdict.risky: Several basics are missing. Run the cheap tests before you spend money.
verdict.rethink: As it stands, this idea is likely to cost more than it earns. Change the weakest parts or try another idea.

evidence.t1: Write a one-page offer with a price and show it to ten people who have the problem.
evidence.t2: Ask for a deposit or a pre-order, not just "would you buy it?".
evidence.t3: Look for people already paying for a clumsy alternative: that is your proof.

price.t1: Find a way to sell more per customer: a bundle, a premium tier or a service on top.
price.t2: Look for a repeat need you can turn into a subscription or regular orders.
price.t3: Test a higher price with the next few customers before you settle on one.

competition.t1: Pick a narrower group the big players ignore (a city, an industry, a style).
competition.t2: Read competitors' one- and two-star reviews and build what they miss.
competition.t3: If nobody sells it, check that people actually search for it or pay for something close.

cost.t1: Start with the smallest version you can sell: one product, one service, one machine.
cost.t2: Rent, borrow or buy used before you buy new equipment.
cost.t3: Pre-sell first and use those orders to pay for stock.

time.t1: Cut the idea down to something you can sell this month.
time.t2: Sell the service by hand before you build the product or the app.
time.t3: Set a date for your first sale and work back from it.

edge.t1: Do three small jobs for friends or at a discount to build the skill and testimonials.
edge.t2: Share what you learn in public to start building an audience.
edge.t3: Partner with someone who has the skill or the customers you lack.

channel.t1: Name the exact place your first ten customers spend time, online or nearby.
channel.t2: Try one channel by hand (posts, messages, a flyer) before paying for ads.
channel.t3: Ask your first customers where they would look for this and go there.

trend.t1: Check how searches and sales for the idea moved over the last few years.
trend.t2: Look for a growing niche inside a shrinking market.
trend.t3: Plan for a market that gets smaller: keep costs flexible and avoid long contracts.
